headlines.title: Bay Area gas prices are on the rise
headlines.description: Gas prices in the Bay Area, along with the rest of California and the nation, keep climbing, according to a weekly fuel report from AAA’s regional office in Walnut Creek. Average fuel prices around the Bay Area include $5.76 in San Francisco, $5.58 in Oakland, and $5.57 in San Jose, according to the statement. At $5.57 per gallon, a 17-cent increase from last week, California had the highest average gas price in the nation, according to the report. “Rising crude oil prices are behind the spike at the pump,” said AAA Mountain West Group spokesperson Aldo Vazquez in a statement. “Volatility along the Strait of Hormuz and instability in the region have pushed oil prices into the $90 per barrel range and could continue driving up costs during the second half of the summer.” The largest component of gas prices at the pump is the cost of crude oil, and the second largest share of retail gas prices is refining costs, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration in the Department of Energy. The price of crude oil on the global market is constantly changing in response to supply, demand, geopolitics and other factors, according to EIA. National gasoline production increased last week, averaging 9.7 million barrels per day, according to EIA. Gasoline demand also increased last week from 8.84 million to 8.94 million barrels per day, which is about 376 million gallons per day. Daily updates of gasoline prices in California, including major metropolitan areas, are available at gasprices.aaa.com.

headlines.title: Sold-out Gilroy Garlic Festival gets underway
headlines.description: The three-day Gilroy Garlic Festival kicked off Friday at the Hecker Pass Outdoor Events Center. This year, 4,000 tickets were made available each day, Friday through Sunday, and they sold out. At this year’s festival, people can enjoy garlic calamari, garlic scampi, pasta con pesto, pepper steak sandwiches, garlic bread, garlic fries, and gourmet all combo plates at the gourmet alley. For those brave enough, there’s also the festival’s famous garlic ice cream. Founded in 1979, the garlic festival has been a staple in California culinary culture, helping to showcase and celebrate the beloved cooking ingredient. In 2017, Guinness World Records certified the festival as the world’s largest garlic festival. In recent years, the festival has faced major challenges. In 2019, three people were killed in a mass shooting and the following year the festival was canceled due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Since then, the festival has faced financial strains and was temporarily shuttered for a couple years before returning in 2025. The Gilroy Garlic Festival Association is a nonprofit organization that has awarded more than $12 million to community schools and service groups, and the entire festival is hosted by volunteers. For more information on the Gilroy Garlic Festival, people can visit gilroygarlicfestival.com. Gilroy 18 hours ago Gilroy Jul 21 Gilroy Garlic Festival returns this weekend
headlines.source: NBC Bay Area staff and Bay City News

headlines.title: 25 arrested during World Cup human trafficking operation in the Bay Area
headlines.description: Authorities conducting human trafficking operations in the Bay Area during the World Cup arrested over two dozen suspected traffickers and provided assistance to dozens of survivors, according to officials. The Santa Clara County District Attorney’s Office on Friday said 53 human trafficking survivors – 42 adults and 11 juveniles – were identified and offered support, 25 suspected traffickers were arrested, and 41 sex buyers were cited during 66 multi-agency operations conducted while World Cup matches were taking place in Santa Clara. “We are proud that Santa Clara County showcased itself to the world so well and so safely, and with one voice declared our intolerance for the illegal trafficking of human beings,” Santa Clara County District Attorney Jeff Rosen said in a statement. “We are standing with the survivors and providing them support and services so that they can go on to live a life free of cruel criminal exploitation.” The survivors were connected with confidential advocates and offered assistance, including safety planning, emergency supplies, blankets, toiletries, temporary housing, and more, the district attorney’s office said. During human trafficking operations earlier this year for Super Bowl LX, which was also held in Santa Clara, authorities arrested 29 suspected traffickers and identified 73 survivors, including 10 minors, according to the district attorney’s office. The World Cup task force consisted of an 11-county regional response team of law enforcement agencies, prosecutors, social workers and advocacy organizations. The team was led by the Santa Clara County Human Trafficking Task Force and the Northern California Regional Intelligence Center, which monitors human trafficking within the Bay Area. The district attorney’s office said the task force used regional coordination for combined intelligence and investigative resources to act instantly during the operations. In one case, undercover investigators sent decoy messages to suspected traffickers, leading 13 to be arrested at various hotels on suspicion of felony pandering. The operation was made up of police departments, human trafficking task forces and sheriff’s offices from cities including San Jose, San Mateo, San Francisco, Mountain View, Hayward, Campbell and Union City. Additionally, the FBI, U.S. Attorney’s Office, Department of State Diplomatic Security Service and California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation assisted in the operation.
headlines.source: NBC Bay Area staff and Bay City News

headlines.title: Big rig crash blocks lanes on I-238 in San Leandro after driver falls asleep
headlines.description: A big rig crash is impacting traffic Friday on Interstate 238 in San Leandro, where lanes won’t be cleared until at least 3 p.m., according to Caltrans officials. The California Highway Patrol said the crash happened shortly before 3:20 a.m. on northbound I-238 just before the interchange with Interstate 880. According to CHP, the truck, which was carrying more than 40,000 pounds of fruit, struck a sand barrel after the driver fell asleep. The impact caused the barrel to explode, scattering sand across the freeway. The truck’s axle was also ripped from underneath the vehicle. Officials said the crash damaged the center median and left sand and fuel in the roadway. No injuries were reported. As of about 12:30 p.m., the number one northbound lane was open, as was the number two lane on the connector to southbound I-880, according to the CHP. Caltrans initially estimated that the crash would be cleared by noon but has pushed that time back to about 3 p.m. Motorists are urged to seek alternate routes. Bay City News contributed to this report
headlines.source: Joel Soria and Bay City News

headlines.title: ICE arrest of Ukrainian woman at SFO captured on video
headlines.description: Video showing a Ukrainian woman being arrested by immigration agents at San Francisco International Airport on Wednesday is drawing attention and raising questions about how the arrest was carried out. This comes alongside a spike in similar stories around the country since June, a trend that has attorneys cautioning their clients not to fly. Video taken of this incident shows a woman in a white shirt and dark pants on the ground outside a store inside SFO, while two men — who appear to be dressed in plainclothes — pin her to the floor. The woman shouts out, “You’re choking me!” and “Please help me!” as people gather around and ask the men what they are arresting her for. At one point, the woman shouts out, “I’m from Ukraine!” Doria Robinson, who happens to be a city council member for the city of Richmond, was in the airport just before 7:45 p.m. that evening. She was waiting to board her flight at the time and recorded video of the incident, which has since been shared by many different accounts across social media. Robinson said she was inside the Harvey Milk Terminal at the B7 gate, already past security, when she heard “a woman screaming at the top of her lungs.” “I looked across, and I saw two men taking a woman who was in a shop across the way, pulling her down to the ground, getting on top of her as she’s screaming,” Robinson recalled. Initially, she said she wondered if it was a domestic violence incident or human trafficking. But as Robinson walked towards the commotion, she realized something else was going on and began recording with her phone. Robinson estimated that hundreds of people around the terminal were also watching this unfold. Robinson said that she did not see the two men wearing any clothing or identification showing who they worked for. Also, she said, despite questions from the crowd about who they were with, the men refused to answer. Ultimately, she said the men handcuffed the woman and carted her away in a wheelchair. A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson confirmed to NBC Bay Area that on July 22, ICE arrested a Ukrainian woman named Iryna Gorb at SFO. The spokesperson added that when officers approached Gorb, “she attempted to flee and resisted arrest.” DHS said Gorb lawfully entered the U.S. in 2010 on a visa that allowed her to stay in the country until the end of May of 2011. DHS said Gorb overstayed her visa and stayed in the U.S. for 15 more years. “She will remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings,” the DHS spokesperson said. Several immigration attorneys told NBC Bay Area they had seen the video of this arrest on social media. “You could hear the fear and the pain in the woman’s voice,” said Bay Area immigration attorney Ghassan Shamieh. Shamieh does not represent Gorb, but said the video was chilling for him to watch. He said that he and other immigration attorneys in his circle have noticed a spike in detentions at airports in the past few weeks. Shamieh said four of his clients have been detained in airports, including one last week at SFO. He added that of his clients who have been detained at airports, none of them have criminal records. “That’s why advocates and immigration attorneys alike are advising clients not to travel via plane even domestically within the United States,” Shamieh said. As for Robinson, she said she is disturbed by this arrest and wonders what will happen to Gorb. “What we do know is we were complicit in it, and there was nothing we could do to help her, and that was just demoralizing, just painful,” Robinson said. A spokesperson for SFO told NBC Bay Area Thursday that the airport doesn’t have any details about this incident “apart from what we’ve seen on social media.” The spokesperson noted that ICE and DHS are federal agencies operating outside the jurisdiction of U.S. airports. “As a result, we are not involved in any decisions about their operations, nor are we notified when they occur,” the spokesperson continued.
headlines.source: Alyssa Goard, Michael Bott and Jessica Gallegos

headlines.title: Bay Area duo sentenced to life for murder of San Mateo rapper
headlines.description: Two men were sentenced to life in prison without parole Wednesday for the murder of a rapper. The killing was part of a chain of retaliatory violence that previously claimed the life of one of the convicted men’s grandmothers, according to the San Mateo County District Attorney’s Office. Ueta Muasika, also known as Juice Boi, died in the shooting in San Mateo on Oct. 30, 2020. According to an 18-month investigation by the San Mateo Police Department, the motive was revenge. Defendant John Paasi had been in the house when Muasika’s cousin Fifita Tau set fire to a San Mateo home in 2019. Tau was targeting members of the West Side Tonga gang, whom he blamed for violence against members of Tau’s family in the Eastside Shoreview Crips gang. While Paasi and five others were rescued, Paasi’s 86-year-old grandmother Susana Tonga did not make it out alive. “I’m make sure Dey feel my pain,” Paasi later wrote on Instagram. On Oct. 30, 2020 at 9:30 a.m., he and co-defendant Isileli Mahe drove to the home of Muasika and fired 14 shots at him and his 2-year-old son. Muasika died at the scene, while his son was shot once in the face but survived after emergency medical treatment. Mahe received a life sentence plus six years, while Paasi, who has a previous charge of burglary, received a life sentence plus 12 years under California’s Three Strikes law. Both had previously been convicted by a jury in March for assault with a semi-automatic firearm and first-degree murder while lying in wait. Lying in wait is a special circumstance under California law that comes with a mandatory sentence of either life in prison without parole or capital punishment. “Justice was done yesterday,” said District Attorney Stephen Wagstaffe. “This was a senseless act that affected the lives of all families, both the families of the victim and the families of the two defendants.” “Not that there’s ever a good reason to take a life. But for this, a minimal motive, they deserve to forfeit their remaining freedom in this lifetime,” Wagstaffe said. Before sentencing, San Mateo County Superior Court Judge Michael Wendler heard victim impact statements from five members of Muasika’s family. Wendler ordered both defendants to pay restitution and both were also ordered to undergo genetic marker testing. Paasi and Mahe’s attorneys did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication.

headlines.title: Valley Fair mall to hold Ed Sheeran lookalike contest before Levi's show
headlines.description: With the FIFA World Cup over, Levi’s Stadium is set to host its first major event since the tournament wrapped up. Ed Sheeran will perform at the Santa Clara venue Saturday night. Drivers should expect heavier traffic beginning Saturday morning as fans head to the concert. For those still hoping to attend, Westfield Valley Fair in San Jose is holding an Ed Sheeran lookalike contest. The grand prize is two floor seats to Saturday night’s show. The contest begins at 1 p.m. Saturday in the mall’s first-floor Center Court. Contestants must RSVP in advance.

headlines.title: 3 Bay Area Little League teams still vying for World Series berths
headlines.description: Three Bay Area youth baseball teams still have hopes of making it to the Little League World Series when they play in the Northern California regional tournament starting this weekend in Chico. Mill Valley Little League, San Ramon Valley Little League and Los Gatos Little League are all competing in the double-elimination NorCal tournament starting Saturday against four other teams in their age bracket for children up to 12 years old. The winner would then also have to win the West Region tournament in San Bernardino in early August to go to the Little League World Series in Williamsport, Pennsylvania. The international tournament brings together some of the best youth baseball teams from countries around the world. Mill Valley won their section tournament in Concord on Tuesday, while San Ramon Valley won theirs the same day in Castro Valley and Los Gatos won theirs Wednesday in Aptos. The NorCal tournament starts Saturday in Chico. Little League’s Intermediate 50/70 World Series for the next age bracket of up to 13-year-olds takes place annually in Livermore and starts Aug. 2. Bollinger Canyon Little League from San Ramon has already qualified as one of the teams competing among six from the U.S. and six internationally at Max Baer Park in Livermore.

headlines.title: Nearly 150,000 mail ballots rejected in California's primary despite efforts to count every vote
headlines.description: Nearly 150,000 California voters had their mail-in ballots rejected for the state’s June primary, a spike from recent elections even as the state attempts to make voting easier with the goal of boosting participation and counting every ballot. California has become notorious for its ponderously slow vote counts that can drag on for weeks and sometimes longer, largely the result of multiple changes over the years that were intended to increase turnout but have done little to achieve that. Among the changes: Every voter receives a mail-in ballot that can arrive at an election office seven days late and still be counted, provided the envelope is postmarked by Election Day. Yet even with that generous weeklong window, the primary driver of the higher rejection numbers is late-arriving ballots, according to data compiled by the secretary of state’s office. Voting experts suspect the main problem is postmarks on ballots that came after Election Day, making them ineligible to be counted. The culprit could be U.S. Postal Service changes that might affect the timing of when postmarks are applied. Late-arriving ballots drove the rejections According to state data, 148,241 mail ballots were rejected in the June election, or a rate of 1.73% of all mail ballots. In raw numbers, that’s up from the 2024 primary, when 108,982 mail ballots were rejected, or a 1.56% rate. In 2022, 105,818 mail ballots were voided during the primary, or a rate similar to 2024. Lateness accounted for 93,479 rejected ballots in June, by far the largest category for disqualifying a ballot. That was up from about 70,000 in the 2022 primary and about 76,000 in the 2024 primary, though turnout in those elections was smaller compared to last June. Kim Alexander, president of the nonpartisan California Voter Foundation, said the jump in rejected ballots because of lateness is a major concern that — along with postal procedures — might also be connected to a late surge in ballots in June. Many voters waited until the final days to make a decision in a wide-open and chaotic race for governor. “Ballots rejected due to lateness are caused primarily to being postmarked too late to count, not because they arrived too late to count,” Alexander wrote in an email. Rejection rates have fluctuated over time, but the growing number of those set aside for lateness compared to recent elections “does really demand the question why this is happening,” said Mindy Romero, director of the Center for Inclusive Democracy, a nonpartisan research group. Lawmakers concerned about USPS postmark changes In January, a group of mostly Democratic U.S. senators sent a letter to the U.S. Postal Service, alarmed that mail-processing changes might affect postmark dates for mail-in ballots during an election year that will determine control of Congress. Updated agency policy says postmarks might not indicate the first day the Postal Service received the mail, but rather the day it was handled in one of its processing centers. Those centers are increasingly likely to be further away from certain communities because of recent consolidations within the Postal Service, which could further delay postmarks. On Thursday, two Wisconsin Democrats, U.S. Sen. Tammy Baldwin and Gov. Tony Evers, called on the Postal Service to address delays that caused hundreds of ballots to arrive after Election Day in the state in April. In June, a federal judge halted President Donald Trump’s executive order that sought to create a federal voter list and limit who can receive a mail ballot. Earlier this year, California election officials urged voters to send their mail ballots early, warning that Postal Service changes could lead to slower mail service. In California, the highest mail ballot rejection rate in June — 3.52% — was in Tulare County, in the agriculture-heavy Central Valley. It was followed by Alpine County, south of Lake Tahoe, and Merced County, also in the Central Valley, which both notched a 3.36% rejection rate. Mismatched signatures and multiple ballots in an envelope Nearly 44,000 ballots were set aside because the voter’s signature didn’t match the one on record with county officials. Over 8,300 ballots were rejected because there was no signature on the returned ballot envelope. In 743 cases, the voter had already cast a ballot, so the mail ballot was voided. Other reasons for rejection included a ballot being missing from the return envelope, or multiple ballots were sent back in a single envelope. The data didn’t break down the uncounted ballots by party registration. Florida, Texas and other large population states quickly wrap up vote counting, while California is a national laggard. After the June primary, President Donald Trump seized on California’s reputation as the national slowpoke in vote counting to renew his long-standing criticism of the state’s elections, while the Republican’s Department of Justice launched an investigation into Los Angeles County’s elections. There is no indication of any widespread problems with mail voting, which has gained in popularity among Democrats and Republicans alike. A report by the Brookings Institution published in 2025 found that the number of cases of mail voting fraud was minuscule — about four cases per 10 million mail ballots.
headlines.source: Michael R. Blood | The Associated Press

headlines.title: With a historic 3 Michelin stars, a Mexican restaurant in San Francisco defies stereotypes
headlines.description: After an eight-year wait, the historic third Michelin star that chef and co-owner Val Cantú and his team at San Francisco’s Californios craved is theirs. It’s the first for a Mexican restaurant anywhere in the world. So it’s understandable he and his 40-person staff have more swagger. “It’s been just really rewarding to see the team kind of like, carry a little bit more confidence in their step,” Cantú told The Associated Press. “Maybe I’ve got some new confidence too.” The feat caps a trajectory that began with Cantú getting his first star right out of the gate when Californios opened in 2015. He got a second one in 2018. At a June ceremony in San Diego, Cantú, with his wife Carolyn by his side, received his third star and a crisp white Michelin chef’s jacket. The accolade feels like validation not just for Californios but for the notion that Mexican food in Mexico and across the diaspora can be an elevated experience. Similar to fine dining Chinese restaurants just a few miles away from Californios, Mexican American restaurants have dealt with criticism for daring to charge more and offering tasting menus. Meanwhile, few bat an eye at French and Japanese restaurants with similar prices. Shoot for the Michelin stars The Michelin Guide, started in 1889 by French brothers Andre and Edouard Michelin, created a star-ranking system in the 1920s. Today, the guide has ratings for over 40,000 restaurants. To evaluate a restaurant, Michelin sends undercover inspectors posing as regular diners. The inspectors said Californios ascended the ranks because it has never been “afraid to cross borders” on the plate, according to Michelin’s website. From the first bite, Californios patrons experience the Texas-born Cantú’s blend of Mexican culture with California ingredients. He starts a meal with a sope, a small hand-formed masa cake made with white corn and beans from a farm in nearby Santa Rosa. Then, with a spatula, caviar made in partnership with a Sacramento sturgeon farm is carefully placed on top. “It’s just really, really delicious and kind of feels like a warm hug,” Cantú said. “It feels comforting.” Michelin inspectors agreed. Californios deserved a three-star promotion, one of five inspectors said on Michelin’s website, for dishes consistently “executed with such precision, refinement and clarity without losing the Mexican identity — things like kombu or the matsukasa yaki fish taco.” Sometimes Cantú and his team would try to guess if a diner could be an inspector. That turned out to be a good reminder that “every guest gets the same quality of presentation and hospitality,” the chef said. Mexican food’s growing recognition comes as immigration enforcement gets harsher In the past few years, Michelin has starred a number of Mexican restaurants including a 10-by-10 foot (3-by-3 meter) taco stand in Mexico City. The growing recognition comes at a precarious time for immigration enforcement policies and the treatment of immigrants — even those in the U.S. legally. Not someone who seeks to inject politics into food, Cantú could not ignore constant headlines about federal immigration operations — some of which have resulted in deaths including a Mexican man in Houston and a Colombian man in Maine earlier this month. Immigrants are “the backbone of all these dish pits and kitchens,” Cantú said. He has shown support through gestures. In March, he collaborated on an “anti-ICE” fundraising dinner. “The culinary world is like a huge supporter of immigrants and the need for immigrants and the need to treat people with respect,” Cantú said. “It’s hard for me to say much more.” Being in a blue state, Cantú is certain most of Californios’ diners share that sentiment. Gustavo Arellano, a food writer and journalist who’s also Mexican American, believes the cuisine’s popularity really helps humanize the immigration debate. “You see this especially like in small Southern towns where the rhetoric is ‘I’m against illegal immigrants. I don’t want too many Mexicans,’” Arellano said. “But, then they look at the Mexican restaurant in town and they’re like ‘Well, not them.’” Californios shows Mexican food is just as worthy of fine dining Growing up, Cantú watched his father and uncle in Texas run a Mexican restaurant and tortillería. As a chef working at high-end establishments in Austin and San Francisco, he found himself asking, “Why is no one doing Mexican cuisine and treating it with like extreme care?” Inspired by the Bay Area, he settled on the name Californios. It’s a nod to descendants of Spanish and Mexican settlers who settled in the 1700s and 1800s in what would become California. Californios started with a $57 four-course tasting menu. The pushback was immediate. “There was a ton of like, ‘This is not Mexican cuisine,’” Cantú said. “Even from our families, you know, trying to explain a contemporary cuisine to a lot of people is totally foreign because people kind of think that cuisine exists in a cookbook and that it doesn’t change.” Californios is at the forefront of what some call “alta California” cuisine, where the children of Mexican immigrants or immigrants themselves use classical chef training with Mexican flavors. The term refers to the former Spanish province north of Baja California; Arellano describes it as an “ideology” that originated in California and has spread across the U.S. Raised flavor profiles and prices ultimately raise skepticism. Arellano argues people think this way partly because they’re trying to keep Mexican food in a box. “There’s always going to be a knee-jerk reaction,” Arellano said. “It goes to this myth that Mexican food should be cheap because Mexicans, all of us are supposedly working class that cannot afford higher-end stuff. That’s classist.” Cantú plans to keep bringing attention to his Mexican-California brand of fine dining. A cookbook is in the works. “Mexican cuisine is one of the most diverse and complex cuisines in the world,” Cantú said, “and there’s countless Mexican immigrants in the United States and Latin immigrants who have their own ideas and concepts of what things can be.” ___ Tang reported from Phoenix.
headlines.source: Terry Tang | The Associated Press and Haven Daley | The Associated Press

headlines.title: San Francisco Zoo welcomes 4 new flamingo chicks, first in nearly a decade
headlines.description: For the first time in nearly a decade, fluffy Chilean flamingo chicks can be seen peeking out from under their parents’ wings at the San Francisco Zoo and Gardens. Over the past week, the zoo’s flamingo flock increased by four — the first successful hatchings in nine years. “The chicks are so far doing well and being cared for by their parents,” said Quinn Brown, the zoo’s curator of birds. On July 11, zoo staff spotted a flamingo egg pipping, part of the natural hatching process when the chick starts to break through the shell. Two days later, the chick could be seen with its mother on a nest mound under her pink feathers. The chick was successfully feeding on the crop milk — a nutritious, bright red liquid produced by both male and female parents, according to the zoo. By Thursday three more chicks had hatched. “There’s nothing sweeter than seeing a flamingo chick having other flamingo chicks to grow up with,” Brown said. The zoo released photos Thursday of fluffy white chicks peeking out from under their parents’ wings and sitting on nest mounds. When the chicks are 3 to 6 months old, during their juvenile phase, they will look more like adult flamingos, except they won’t be fully pink. They learn how to filter feed on their own, ingesting foods rich in beta-carotene. As adults from 3 to 5 years old they start to turn pale pink, turning to deep pink as they mature, the zoo said. Guests can see the Chilean flamingo chicks at the Flamingo Lake habitat located at the end of Zoo Street by the Leaping Lemur Cafe. The four new chicks come after the zoo made adjustments to the flamingos’ environment over the past several months, installing a mesh netting enclosure over the habitat. The mesh enclosure means the flock can stay outside at night, rather than inside their night quarters, allowing them to act more naturally. Before, the birds were brought inside at night to protect against wild predators and as a hedge against avian flu. It kept the birds safe, but the flamingos weren’t likely to nest since they stay on nest mounds for more than 30 days. “We had no expectations of chicks this year, but wanted to see if they would behave differently since they had unlimited outdoor access,” Brown said. Flamingo keeper Liz Gibbons observed some behavioral changes in the flock in April. The next month, staff started prepping the flamingo habitat’s beach area to provide the best conditions possible for the flock to nest build. To prep the mounds, staff used Dura Edge’s Dura Pitch, the same brand of dirt used in Major League Baseball stadiums, including the San Francisco Giants. They also added extra dirt to nearby flat surfaces. Staff spent hours building cone-shaped mounds, for the flamingos to use or build their nests with the extra added substrate between the water and the fence. Soon after the manmade mounds were built, flamingo pairs opted to build their nests in one of the corners of the habitat, close to the public viewing area. To allow them their nesting time with limited disruptions, staff cordoned off part of the closest viewing area with a tiki-shading, allowing them privacy.

headlines.title: San Francisco lags behind in preparedness for extreme heat events
headlines.description: Although San Francisco’s nickname is “Fog City” and it’s famous for its cool summers, it’s not immune to occasional heat waves. City infrastructure and residents may not be adequately adapted and ready to deal with extreme heat when it does occur, according to the San Francisco Department of Public Health. “We often think of ourselves as a city of fog and jackets, and for most of our history, that has been true,” said Board of Supervisors President Rafael Mandelman at a hearing Thursday. “But it has also left us unprepared for very hot days. Our bodies never build a tolerance for heat because our hot days are rare.” Mandelman held the hearing to evaluate the city’s readiness for handling extreme heat, revealing a lack of city preparedness to deal with soaring temperatures. “This is a huge problem,” he said. “It seems very, very important to move quickly and do something.” Extreme heat is the most dangerous weather-related event in the United States, killing more Americans than other weather events like floods and hurricanes. In 2017, three people in San Francisco died when the temperature reached a record 106 degrees Fahrenheit. The hearing, which addressed the city’s position in being prepared and responsive to hot weather, was held during a Board of Supervisors Public Safety and Neighborhood Services Committee meeting. It came as temperatures reached 85 degrees Fahrenheit on Tuesday — the city’s hottest July day in 11 years. Earlier this year, temperatures broke the all-time March temperature record when the city hit 90 degrees Fahrenheit. “As our climate changes, extreme heat events are becoming more frequent,” said University of California, San Francisco faculty member Dr. Neeta Thakur at the hearing. “Compared to two decades ago, we’re seeing almost twice as more heat events in the last decade here in San Francisco.” Only about one third of households in the city have central air conditioning, Mandelman said. While cooling centers can help, UCSF researchers found that they are not used by many. “Climate resilience needs to meet people where they are,” Thakur said. “It requires investing in the homes, buildings, and the neighborhood infrastructures that allow people, especially those least able to adapt, to remain safe where they live.” In 2021, the Office of Resilience and Capital Planning and the Department of Public Health created the Heat and Air Quality Resilience Project with the objective to plan, identify, and implement strategies across city departments aimed at reducing health impacts during high heat events. Representatives from ORCP and DPH identified inadequate infrastructure like air conditioning and limited resources to implement the new infrastructure as major issues stalling the city in its goals toward heat resilience. “I think I’m pretty worried,” said Matt Wolff, DPH’s Climate Health Program manager. While there has been some implementation of low-cost air conditioning in about 90 community sites and facilities, the Department of Emergency Management, or DEM, has not been able to secure competitive grant funding to expand that effort. “Even though it’s a really successful proof of concept for what this can look like, DEM currently doesn’t have the capacity to kind of scale up the intervention,” said Alex Morrison, an analyst at the Office of Resilience and Capital Planning. The Heat and Air Quality Resilience Project also found that residents in rental units have more challenges in getting air conditioning installed. “The largest obstacle that residents face is actually making changes to their living spaces, largely because they’re renters,” Morrison said. Another way that the city is trying to be more heat resilient is through decarbonization to help reduce climate change. A lack of resources and investment in moving buildings away from fossil fuels has slowed down the city’s pace toward reducing greenhouse gas emissions. “The things that we need to do now are harder,” said the Environment Department’s Climate Program Manager Cyndy Comerford. “They’re more complex, and they require more resources.” DEM Executive Director Mary Ellen Carroll said that her department is “very well positioned to respond to a heat event.” She said that DEM has resources like emergency notifications, information alerts, and community education on preparedness. “We are in the crisis,” Carroll said. “We are in the eye of the storm, we are going to continue to have these events, and it is important that we prepare.” After about two hours of discussion, Mandelman asked to continue the hearing to a later meeting. “We have the map now, but we don’t have the resources to actually go down the path and get to the place we want to go,” he said.
